blemish

/BLEM-ish/ - the stress falls on BLEM · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Blemish means a small imperfection on a surface — a mark that spoils the look while leaving the thing sound underneath.

The saddler works around every blemish in the hide rather than cutting through one.

Example

The used-car buyer circled the sedan twice and found a single blemish — a pea-sized dimple on the trunk lid — and talked four hundred dollars off the price for it.

Blemish is the precise word because the mark is small, superficial, and spoils only the look: the car runs perfectly. A dent that changed how the trunk closed would be damage; a blemish just interrupts an otherwise clean surface.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flaw: A flaw is any defect at all, inside or out — a crack in a casting, a hole in an argument. A blemish stays on the surface: a small mark that spoils only the look of a thing while leaving it perfectly sound underneath.

imperfection: Imperfection is the broadest, mildest word for falling short of perfect, and it needn't be visible at all — a wobbly chord, a rough draft. A blemish is specific: a small visible mark on an otherwise clean surface, skin, fruit, paint, or a reputation.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enhancement: a change that improves the look instead of marring it

perfection: the flawless state a blemish interrupts

Where it sits · how deeply the surface is damaged — smudge → blemish → gash

smudge vs. blemish: A smudge is milder than a blemish — it wipes away and leaves the surface unharmed.

gash vs. blemish: A gash goes further than a blemish: the surface itself is cut open, not merely marked.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — blemish

Root — blemish: whole-word borrowing from Old French ble(s)mir, to make pale, to injure

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: blemish came into English whole, from an Old French verb meaning 'to make pale, to injure.' A blemish was originally the pale bruise-mark an injury left behind — and the word still names the small mark that spoils a surface.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Old French ble(s)mir left exactly one descendant in modern English — blemish itself. Its root survives nowhere else, so there is no cousin word to build; the history lives in this single word for the mark an injury leaves.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral

Blemish is for small, surface-level faults — on skin, fruit, paint, or, figuratively, on a record or reputation. If the defect runs deeper than the surface, flaw is the stronger, broader word; if it can simply be wiped away, it was only a smudge.
